title: Favor composition over inheritance
concept: Inheritance is a powerful way to achieve code reuse, but it violates encapsulation when used across package boundaries on classes not explicitly designed and documented for extension. In an implementation inheritance relationship, the subclass depends on the implementation details of its superclass. If the superclass changes across releases (e.g. self-use of methods or adding new methods that collide with subclass invariants), the subclass can silently break. The solution is Composition: instead of extending an existing class, give your new class a private field referencing an instance of the existing class, and forward method calls.

when_to_use_flashcard.front: When should you use inheritance vs composition?
when_to_use_flashcard.back: Inheritance is appropriate ONLY when a genuine 'is-a' relationship exists AND the subclass and superclass are in the same package or the superclass was specifically designed and documented for extension. In all other cases, favor composition ('has-a').

when_not_to_use_flashcard.front: What is the 'self-use' problem in implementation inheritance?
when_not_to_use_flashcard.back: When a superclass method internally calls another of its own methods (e.g. `addAll` calling `add`). If a subclass overrides both, the subclass method may execute twice, causing double counting or invariant corruption.

quiz.question: Why did `InstrumentedHashSet.addAll()` double-count elements in the classic Effective Java example?
options: HashSet's addAll method is implemented on top of its add method (self-use), which InstrumentedHashSet also overrode
HashSet creates two copies of each element
The JVM does not support overriding addAll()
It was executed concurrently by two threads

quiz.question: What is the design pattern name for a class that holds an instance of another class and forwards method invocations to it with added behavior?
options: Decorator (or Wrapper) pattern
Singleton pattern
Abstract Factory pattern
Flyweight pattern

quiz.question: What is the only known disadvantage of wrapper classes (composition with forwarding)?
options: The 'SELF problem': the wrapped object does not know about the wrapper, so callbacks pass references to the inner object instead of the wrapper
Wrapper classes consume 10x more heap memory
They cannot implement interfaces
They prevent garbage collection

quiz.question: Which standard Java library class notoriously violated 'favor composition over inheritance' by extending Vector instead of wrapping it?
options: java.util.Stack
java.util.ArrayList
java.util.HashMap
java.util.LinkedList

quiz.question: What question should an architect ask before deciding to extend class B with class A?
options: Is every A genuinely and unconditionally a B? ('is-a' test)
Is A larger in memory than B?
Does B have more than three methods?
Can B be serialized to JSON?

interview_questions.question: Why does implementation inheritance violate encapsulation?
interview_questions.model_answer: In implementation inheritance, a subclass is inextricably tied to the internal execution details of its superclass. If the author of the superclass changes how methods invoke one another (self-use) or adds new methods that conflict with subclass security policies or invariants, the subclass breaks silently through no fault of its own.

interview_questions.question: Why is `java.util.Properties` extending `java.util.Hashtable<Object, Object>` considered one of Java's worst design flaws?
interview_questions.model_answer: `Properties` is intended to store only String key-value pairs. Because it extends `Hashtable` rather than wrapping it, clients can call `properties.put(key, nonStringObject)` directly through the inherited `Hashtable` interface, corrupting internal properties invariants and breaking methods like `getProperty()`.

interview_questions.question: What is the 'SELF problem' with wrapper classes?
interview_questions.model_answer: When a wrapped inner object passes `this` to a callback framework or event listener, it passes a reference to itself, completely bypassing the wrapper. If the client expects wrapper behaviors during callbacks, those behaviors are missed.

interview_questions.question: How does the Wrapper pattern provide vastly greater flexibility than subclassing a specific collection class?
interview_questions.model_answer: An `InstrumentedSet<E>` wrapper that implements `Set<E>` can instrument *any* `Set` implementation (e.g. `HashSet`, `TreeSet`, `ConcurrentSkipListSet`, or custom sets), whereas a subclass only instruments the single class it statically extends.
